title: Calm in the Character of God: Omnipresence
speaker: Elder Nick Anderson
summary: This lesson concludes a series on God's character and anxiety by exploring God's omnipresence—His constant, everywhere presence—and how this truth provides comfort and eliminates the need for worry. Through biblical examples and practical application, the speaker demonstrates that believers can trust in God's nearness during times of crisis, and addresses three ways to seek God's kingdom: looking upward to God's character, looking outward to serve others in community, and looking forward to eternal hope in heaven.

outline.title: God's Omnipresence: Always Present Everywhere
subpoints: God is everywhere present in His fullness, not withdrawn or distant from creation
God sustains every molecule of the universe; creation depends on His continuous presence
There is no place where God is absent (Psalm 139:7-12)
To believers, God's omnipresence is ultimate comfort; to unbelievers, ultimate terror

outline.title: God Is a Very Present Help in Trouble
subpoints: God is our refuge and strength in the midst of chaos and difficulty (Psalm 46:1)
The Christian life is impossible to live on our own strength; we must depend on God's strength
Biblical examples of the impossible made possible through God's presence: Moses, Elijah, David, Daniel, Hezekiah
When we are weak, Christ's strength is made perfect in us (2 Corinthians 12:10)

outline.title: Faith, Not Fear: The Case of Elisha's Servant
subpoints: When surrounded by the army of Assyria, Elisha's servant saw only the threat
Elisha prayed for God to open his servant's eyes to see God's army of protection
God's presence and power are real even when we cannot see them
We must choose between faith and fear; there are only two options
God's omnipresence to believers means He is with us in a unique, special way

outline.title: The Command: Seek First the Kingdom of God
subpoints: Jesus commands us not to worry, but also commands us to seek His kingdom (Matthew 6)
We are not freed from anxiety by doing nothing; work is part of the antidote
Good theology must lead to obedience and good works
Service to God is both corrective and healing for anxiety

outline.title: Look Upward: Know the Character of God
subpoints: Study Scripture, memorize Scripture, know the stories of God's character and action
Build up your faith through knowledge of who God is
When crisis comes, you will know that God is your refuge
Example: Hezekiah faced Sennacherib's army but knew God's character and prayed rather than panicking

outline.title: Look Outward: Serve Others in Community
subpoints: We are not isolated individuals; we are part of the body of Christ
Looking outward to serve others is part of God's design for dealing with anxiety
The early church was devoted to each other: confessing sins, forgiving, serving, bearing burdens together
An individualistic mentality prevents us from experiencing the fullness of Christian community
We confess sins to one another, forgive one another, serve one another, build one another up
Isolation robs us and others of the blessings God promises in community (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10)

outline.title: Look Forward: Set Your Mind on Eternal Hope
subpoints: This world is passing away; our eternal home with Christ is forever
Set your mind on things above, not on earthly things (Colossians 3:1-4)
Heaven is imperishable, undefiled, unfading, tearless, free from temptation and sin
We should look forward to our reward in heaven, as Moses and Abraham did
Our earthly troubles are temporary compared to eternal glory
When heaven is your home, worry about earthly things loses its grip

transcript:
## God's Character and Anxiety: Omnipresence

We are continuing and concluding our series on God's character and anxiety today. We had eight or nine lessons—I lost track of how many there are. But Pastor Tito Lyro gave us a good introduction on the idea of anxiety and how we as Christians ought to think about anxiety because we have competing worldviews. We have a biblical worldview and then we have the world's worldview. We were encouraged to think about anxiety the way God tells us to think about anxiety. Anxiety is not a thing that happens to us. It's our response to the world around us. Anxiety and worry are a sinful response. Jesus told us, do not worry. There are lots of commands that tell us do not worry. If we do the things that we're told not to do, we call that sin. So worry is a sin.

Scott Hollander talked about God as our Father. I talked earlier about the immutability of God. We talked about omniscience, sovereignty, the love of God, and the God who hears and answers prayers. And today we will talk about God's omnipresence. And then if I have time, we'll try to wrap it up with a little bit of application from our book.

## The Crisis All Around Us

We have trouble all around us, don't we? We have wars going on in Iran, Israel, Lebanon, Gaza, Ukraine, and other places that we don't even think about. We have economic hardships all around us. Oil and gas prices are going up. Housing prices are going up. Food prices are going up. There's even talk about the risk of famine in certain parts of the world because of the wars that are going on. There are always risks around us. We have personal crises. We have cancer diagnoses, illnesses, disease, chronic issues that we're all dealing with. We have job losses sometimes. We have interpersonal conflict.

There are all kinds of things going on around us that we can respond to with worry and anxiety. Yet none of this surprises God. He tells us in Ecclesiastes that there is nothing new under the sun. God is not surprised by what's going on. Indeed, He's ordained what is going on.

In our final lesson here, we're going to talk about omnipresence and anxiety and how that helps us with our anxiety.

## What Is Omnipresence?

Omnipresence is a fancy theological word meaning that God is always present everywhere. Not that God is in everything or that everything is a part of God. We're not pantheistic, but God is everywhere present at all times. Not like the oxygen that is always around us or like molecules that are everywhere, but God in the fullness of His divine being and power is there everywhere all the time.

God did not create the universe and then wind it up like a clock. God did not wind up the universe and then just let it run and be disinterested. We're not deists either. God is ever present, ever interested, ever controlling every moment of all time. He's always there. God is active. He sustains every molecule of the universe at every moment in time. If God were to withdraw His power, withdraw His presence, the creation would just cease to exist.

There's no place where you can go where God is absent. Psalm 139, verses 7 through 12, says this:

> "Where can I go from Your Spirit? Or where can I flee from Your presence? If I ascend into heaven, You're there. If I make my bed in hell, behold, You are there. If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there Your hand shall lead me and Your right hand shall hold me. If I say surely the darkness shall fall on me, even the night shall be light about me. Indeed, the darkness shall not hide from You, but the night shines as the day. The darkness and the light are both alike to You." (Psalm 139:7-12)

R.C. Sproul says there is no place where God is not. You cannot hide from Him. You cannot escape Him. To the believer, this is the ultimate comfort. To the unbeliever, it is the ultimate terror. And that's what we're going to focus on today: that God is uniquely present to the believer.

This is what Jesus meant when He said, "I am with you always." Not just that He, God, is everywhere present, but that He is in a unique way present to the believer at all times and all places.

## God Is Our Refuge and Strength

Psalm 46 begins with this statement:

> "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear, even though the earth be removed and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea, though its waters roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with its swelling." (Psalm 46:1-3)

God is your refuge and your strength. Not could be or might be or was, but He is at all times. He is your refuge and strength.

Let me tell you something that's going to shock you. The Christian faith is not difficult. It's impossible. You cannot live the Christian faith on your own. There's a saying that goes around: "God never gives you more than you can handle." And I would argue that is wrong—at least in the sense that you cannot live this life on your own strength. It requires the strength of another, namely God.

Was Moses able to part the Red Sea on his own? Was Moses able to make water come out of the rock on his own? Was Elijah able to defeat the prophets of Baal on his own strength? Did David beat Goliath by his own strength? Did the walls of Jericho fall because the army of Israel was so strong? Was Daniel able to close the mouths of the lions in the lion's den? Did Hezekiah defeat Sennacherib by his own strength? No. All of these things were too much for men to handle, and yet God made them happen. Sometimes God does bring things into your life that you can't handle on your own, but He can, and He teaches us to trust in Him through those things.

Peter was the one who boasted about his own faith, and yet he was the one who denied Christ three times. Paul, on the other hand, did not boast in his own strength. He wrote in 2 Corinthians 12:10:

> "Therefore I take pleasure in my infirmities, in reproaches, in needs, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ's sake, for when I am weak, then I am strong." (2 Corinthians 12:10)

When we come to the end of our own strength, it turns us to God.

Psalm 27 says:

> "The Lord is my strength and my shield, my heart trusted in Him, and I am helped. Therefore, my heart greatly rejoices, and with my song I will praise Him." (Psalm 27:1)

We, however, like Peter, have a tendency to trust in ourselves and to boast in ourselves. We trust in our own resources, we trust in our own wisdom, we trust in our retirement fund, we trust in all kinds of things. Yet the Bible tells us this in Isaiah 40, verses 29 through 31:

> "He gives power to the weak, and to those who have no might, He increases strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall, but those who wait on the Lord will renew their strength. They shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint." (Isaiah 40:29-31)

We are not strong. Ephesians 6:10 tells us:

> "Be strong in the Lord and in the power of His might." (Ephesians 6:10)

The term "Lord of hosts" is used some 250 times in the Old Testament. He is a warrior—that's what that means. He is the commander of the armies of heaven. He is a warrior, and He is omnipresent. He is with you in a special way.

## Elisha's Servant: A Lesson in Faith and Fear

We have a great example of this in Elisha's servant. Do you remember the story of Elisha's servant? The king of Assyria is at war with Israel, and he sends his army to capture Elisha at Dothan. While they're there in the city, the army surrounds the city. 2 Kings 6, verses 14 through 16, records this for us:

> "And when the servant of the man of God arose early and went out, there was an army surrounding the city with horses and chariots. And his servant said to him, 'Alas, my master, what shall we do?' So he answered him, 'Do not fear, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.' Remember it's just the two of them there. That's all the servant can see. He says, 'Those who are with us are more than those who are with them.' And Elisha prayed and said, 'Lord, I pray open his eyes that he may see.' Then the Lord opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw. And behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha." (2 Kings 6:14-17)

That is the God who was with you. The same God who surrounded the city with horses and chariots to protect Elisha is the God who was with you in your trouble. The servant of Elisha was afraid because he couldn't see that. He could not see that God, the Lord of hosts, was with them. Elisha wasn't afraid though. He knew the battle was already won. He believed what Psalm 55:22 says:

> "Cast your burden on the Lord and he shall sustain you. He shall never permit the righteous to be moved." (Psalm 55:22)

The Bible commands us: be anxious for nothing. Elisha was surrounded by an army. Speaking strictly in human terms, he had a very good reason to be anxious. At least that's what we would think. You're in a city, you and your servant, and you're surrounded by an army. If there's any time to worry, again, just thinking in human terms, that would probably be a good time to worry, wouldn't it? But Elisha was not worried because he knew what Psalm 46 says—that God is our refuge and strength.

So the question for us today is: What is our response going to be when, figuratively speaking, we are surrounded by an army and it's just us and a servant? Are we going to believe what Psalm 46 says or not? Do we believe or do we live in fear? We either have faith or we have fear. Those are the two options that we have.

If we know who God is, what reason can we possibly have to be worried? When everything falls apart around us, when it just seems like there's chaos, we are able by the work of the Lord in our hearts to respond with faith and not with fear.

So the question today is: Is God your refuge? And for the believer, it is a resounding yes. He is your refuge. But do you believe that? Are you trusting in that? Are you trusting in Him?

## Don't Be Anxious; Bring Your Requests to God

We've referenced Philippians 4:6-7 in the series several times already, and that says:

> "Be anxious for nothing but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving. Let your requests be made known to God and the peace of God which surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:6-7)

What we sometimes miss is what verse 5 says. Right before it tells us, "Don't be anxious, bring everything to God," verse 5 tells us:

> "The Lord is near." (Philippians 4:5)

So don't be anxious, bring your requests to Him. Why? Because the Lord is near.

## Psalm 46: Complete Text

If you want to turn to Psalm 46, I'm going to read the whole psalm:

> "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear, even though the earth be removed and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea. Though the waters roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with its swelling. There is a river whose streams shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacle of the Most High. God is in the midst of her. She shall not be moved. God shall help her just at the break of dawn. The nations raged, the kingdoms were moved, he uttered his voice, the earth melted. The Lord of hosts is with us. The God of Jacob is our refuge. Come behold the works of the Lord who has made desolations in the earth. He makes wars cease to the end of the earth. He breaks the bow and cuts the spear in two. He burns the chariot in the fire. Be still and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted in the earth. The Lord of hosts is with us. The God of Jacob is our refuge." (Psalm 46)

Look at verse 2. It says: "Therefore we will not fear even though the earth be removed and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." As I was reading this, I was picturing going outside and seeing Mount Rainier just being thrown into the ocean. The psalm just talks about absolute chaos. "Though the waters roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with its swelling." And yet we are able to trust in God and not be worried even though there is just chaos going on all around us.

Again, imagine being in a city surrounded by an army. And Psalm 46 is your refuge. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. In the midst of this chaos all around you, God says in verse 10:

> "Be still and know that I am God." (Psalm 46:10)

I don't think our natural reaction to chaos is to be still. Our natural reaction is to be very active, worried, and anxious. And yet God says, be still and know that I am God. Whatever you're going through, when life is falling apart, God is not. God is not falling apart. He's not caught by surprise by whatever it might be—a job loss, relationship conflict, death, whatever it is. God already knows and He's there. He is a present help in trouble.

## What Do We Do? Three Directives

So what do we do as a result of what we've learned in this series? That's the next question. We read Matthew 6 quite a few times and we see that Jesus tells us that He watches the sparrow, considers the lilies and how they're dressed. Even Solomon was not dressed like that. He says, don't worry. But the danger we have is that we don't do what He tells us to do after He says, "Do not worry." He tells us not to worry, but then He says something else that we're supposed to do in response, and that is:

> "Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness." (Matthew 6:33)

Seek first the kingdom of heaven. Jesus didn't say, okay, don't worry. God's in control. Just sit there. God does not tell us just to sit there and don't worry. Just trust me. I'll take care of it. You don't need to do anything. He says, no, don't worry. Trust in me. And by the way, there's work to be done. Go do it. Seek first the kingdom of heaven. He tells us to get busy.

We're not freed from anxiety by doing nothing. The work that we are supposed to do is part of the antidote for anxiety. Good theology leads to obedience and we are to be full of good works. Seek first means not only put your faith in Christ, but become more like Christ and grow in obedience to Christ. Service to God is Jesus' prescription here. It is corrective for us and it is healing for us.

I think there are three ways that we can seek first the kingdom of God. The first one: look upward, look outward, and look forward.

### Look Upward: Know Who God Is

The first one is look upward. We've actually talked about this aspect for the vast majority of this series. We look upward. We lift our gaze from the chaos around us and we look to who God is. We look to the character of God.

Hezekiah—you remember what happened to Hezekiah? The army of Assyria, Sennacherib, destroyed 46 fortified cities and then he surrounded Jerusalem and he had a massive army with him. He tells Hezekiah and the people there: "No other god has been able to defeat my army and there is no way that your God is going to defeat my army."

Hezekiah could have stood on the walls of Jerusalem and wrung his hands and got worried and anxious and just looked at the army and thought, "What am I possibly going to do here?" Now Assyria was famous for their ability to siege walled fortified cities. They would build mounds made up of just earth and rubble and rock and stuff so that they could get up over the top of the walls. They had a very sophisticated way of sieging these cities. Sometimes they would dig underneath the walls to make the walls actually crumble so that the wall was effectively useless.

So this is not like some army showed up and they don't have any kind of reputation. They were famous for taking out fortified cities and Hezekiah knew this. And yet he didn't panic. He did exactly what we ought to do whenever we are surrounded by an army. He got on his knees and he prayed to God. He looked upward. He knew the character of God. He knew that God is an ever present help in trouble.

First and foremost, and this is what we've been talking about for the majority of this series: First and foremost we need to know who God is. We need to know the character of God. We need to not just read our Bible but study our Bible, to love our Bible, to memorize our Bible so that when things come to us we know, "Oh, God is our very present help in trouble. God can do this." We need to know the stories of the Bible. There's a reason we teach the stories of the Bible because we need to know how God acts. We need to know what He is like to build up our faith so that when something happens we don't panic.

So that's how we look upward.

### Look Outward: Serve Others in Community

Secondly, we need to look outward. We need to remember that we are not the only child of God in this world. Other people matter. This life is not about us. Instead of staring at our own problems, we need to train ourselves to look outward to the people around us and ask the question: How can I serve them?

You remember Elijah on Mount Carmel? He defeated the prophets of Baal. That was like the high point of his ministry. It was a great victory. And then what did he do right after that? He ran away. He ran away because Jezebel was trying to capture and kill him. He ran away and he started to mope and feel bad for himself because he thought that he was alone. But when God spoke to him, He didn't just comfort him. He told him, "Okay, there's work to be done. Go and do the work that I've told you to go do."

A solitary existence is not how we deal with anxiety and worry. When we're anxious, we are far more inclined to retreat into ourselves rather than to serve other people. And we justify it. We say to ourselves, "Well, I'm so worried. I just don't have the bandwidth to deal with anyone else's problems." But that's actually how God helps us deal with our anxiety and our worries—by serving other people. Elijah was depressed because Jezebel wanted to kill him and yet God sent him to do more work.

We live in a very individualistic society and that's not a good thing. We cannot implement the truths of the Bible if we have an individualistic mentality. We hurt together and we grow together and that's the way God designed it. Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 says:

> "Two are better than one because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, one will lift up his companion, but woe to him who is left alone when he falls, for he has no one to help him up." (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10)

Brothers and sisters, our burdens are the heaviest when we are trying to carry them on our own. So if you have an inclination or a tendency to isolate yourself, that's not a healthy thing and, at least in one sense, it's disobedience to the scripture.

In Acts 2:42 it says there's this young church that's just been formed:

> "They continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship in the breaking of bread and in prayers." (Acts 2:42)

Fellowship was so important that Luke decided he needed to record that they were following the apostles' doctrines, they were having fellowship with each other, they were breaking bread and they were praying together. The early church was devoted to each other. Everywhere there is a healthy church, you're going to find the people in that church being devoted to each other—not just asking how can I get served today.

Think about this: If everyone in this room came to church today thinking, "How am I going to get served today?" who gets served? No one. Yet if everyone shows up today and thinks, "How can I serve someone else?" who gets served? Everyone gets served. Selfishness is not a good thing. Coming to church and thinking, "How am I going to get served? How am I going to get fed today?" is a wrong mentality and it's epidemic across Christianity at least in the United States. We need to come to church and ask ourselves: How can I be a blessing to someone else today?

This early church was devoted to each other and this is expressed in many different ways in the scriptures.

First, we are to confess our sins to each other. I just made everyone uncomfortable but that's what the scripture says. We are supposed to confess our sins to one another. We confess our sins to God as well, but we are also commanded to confess our sins to each other. You can't practice that if you are on your own, if you have an individualistic, "it's just Jesus and me" mentality.

Number two goes along with this: we are to forgive one another. Yes, we are going to fail each other. We are going to hurt each other at times and yet we have to be ready to forgive each other. We are commanded to forgive one another. Again, you can't forgive other people if there are no other people in your life.

We are to serve one another. The Lord's Prayer does not begin with the word "my." It begins: "Our Father in heaven." Jesus assumes that we are practicing our faith with other people.

We are to stimulate others to love and good works. Sometimes we need to stimulate other people to do what is right. Sometimes we need to be stimulated by other people to do what is right. Neither of those is going to happen if we are not in community with each other.

We are to bear one another's burdens. We are to be with other people when they are going through difficulties and we need people to be with us when we are going through difficulties.

We are to love one another. God has given us to each other so that we can express the love of Christ right here and now.

We need to build one another up and we need to teach one another. Sometimes we need to be the person teaching, sometimes we need to be the person being taught. Again, none of this can happen if we think it's just me and Jesus. How can I get served today?

So we need to look outward to other people. For those who really like being solitary, consider that when we are disconnected from other believers we are robbing both ourselves and them of all of the blessings that God promises to us when we live in a community of believers.

### Look Forward: Set Your Mind on Heaven

And finally we look forward. We look forward to our eternal home. When we see that this world is passing away, it's contrasted with the fact that our eternal home is just that—it's eternal, and the Lord is preparing a place for us. Your eternal future is with Christ. He will take us to be with him someday and that ought to be more than enough for us with whatever we are going through.

Colossians 3:1-4 says:

> "If then you were raised with Christ, seek those things which are above where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God. Set your mind on things above, not on things on the earth, for you died and your life is hidden with Christ and God. When Christ who is our life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory." (Colossians 3:1-4)

So what is your mind set on today? Is it set on temporary things or is it set on the eternal? What are the things that you think about constantly? What are the things that you worry about constantly? And how often do you actually take a moment out of your busy day and think about: Where am I going when I die? It's going to happen to all of us unless the Lord comes. We're going somewhere. We're going to heaven or we're going to hell and we need to think about it.

Now I'm not a big fan of the theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, but I remember. He was faithful in that he stayed in Germany when the Nazis took over and he was part of the resistance. He was one of the very few pastors who actually stayed there. Most of them either capitulated or left. And I remember I took a class on him in college and one of the things that stood out to me was that he and his sister every night when they were going to bed would talk about what heaven was going to be like. And I've got to believe that that had some kind of influence on his life and the fact that he was willing to stay in Germany and minister to the Christians who were there despite all the risks. And eventually he died because he stayed there.

So what is your mind set on? Do we spend time thinking about heaven? About what it's going to be like when we're there with Christ? Do we think about how long eternity is going to be compared to how short this life is? We might have 70, 80, 90 years. But how long is eternity? It doesn't end. We're going to be there for trillions and trillions and trillions and trillions of years. We can't even fathom how long that's going to be. This life is just a breath and it's gone. And yet we're so worried about our bank account balance.

But when you put things in those terms, it really brings it into balance, doesn't it? It makes us realize that this life is significant in the way that it has eternal consequences and yet the things that we worry about are so small. And God is present with us. He knows the things that we struggle with.

I'm not trying to minimize the very real difficulties we go through. Yet sometimes they're overblown in our minds because we haven't thought about where are we going? Where does this journey end? It ends in heaven. And that's why we can bear the things that we go through.

Heaven is an imperishable place. It's never going to be destroyed. It's undefiled. There's no sin. It's unfading. It's tearless. It's a holy place. It's free from temptation. Just that thought—just being free from temptation is a wonderful thought. Our Father is there. Our Lord is there. Our inheritance is there. What belongs to Christ belongs to us because we are His children. And our heavenly reward is there.

And this is going to make you uncomfortable. We should look forward to our reward. Moses and Abraham were motivated by their reward. That seems wrong, doesn't it? It feels icky to think that we're going to be rewarded. But the scriptures tell us there is a reward for you in heaven and you ought to look forward to that reward.

Hebrews 11:24-26 says this:

> "By faith Moses, when he became of age refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasure of sin, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater than the treasures in Egypt, for he looked to the reward." (Hebrews 11:24-26)

And then Hebrews 11:10, talking about Abraham, says:

> "For he waited for the city which has foundations whose builder and maker is God." (Hebrews 11:10)

We often point to the heroes of the faith—rightfully so—Moses, Abraham, David, and all the others. They were people who looked for the reward. They were looking forward to heaven. And we are told in the Sermon on the Mount:

> "Don't store up treasure on earth where moth and rust destroy. It doesn't stop there. It says store up treasure in heaven." (Matthew 6:19-20)

So we are to look for the reward. And that is being with Christ in heaven. Christ is our greatest reward. Our greatest joy is in heaven. Spurgeon said: "The best moment of a Christian's life is his last one because it is the one that is nearest heaven." We will have pleasures forevermore in heaven.

So if heaven is your home, I'll leave you with us. If heaven is your home, why are you so worried about the things on earth?
